description: What a continuous scale does with a value that is not a number, which is one line of d3 and two rules: `return x == null || isNaN(x = +x) ? unknown : …`. **Nothing is caught before the coercion** — a null and an undefined answer `unknown`, which is `undefined` unless the scale was given one — and **everything else goes through `+`**, which is `Number(x)` and not a parse: the empty string is `0`, an empty array is `0`, a flag is `1`, and only a word that is not a number reaches `NaN` and so `unknown` as well. The rows below are those five cases and a plain number to hold the axis. The empty cell is the one that matters in practice, a column read from a CSV being full of them: upstream places it at zero and this engine dropped it, because its coercion read a string with `toDoubleOrNull` — a *parse*, which rejects the empty string where `Number` accepts it. The symbols are drawn at the value's own position and labelled with what the scale answered, so a row that is placed and a row that is not are told apart by the text rather than by an absence. An **ordinal** scale is asked the same questions last: it has no coercion at all — its index is keyed by the value — so every one of these is a miss, and a miss answers `unknown` exactly as the others do. It is here because it is the one scale family whose answer for a value it cannot place is reached without any arithmetic, which makes it the clearest statement of what `unknown` is. The last scale has an **empty range**, which is legal and answers `unknown` for everything — even for a value its domain does hold, there being nothing to answer with: `range[index % 0]` is `range[NaN]`. It is asked about a value in its domain rather than outside it, so the branch it pins is the empty range and not the miss. A **log** scale is asked the same questions, and it is the one that says which side the guard is on: `x == null || isNaN(x = +x)` tests the **input**, and the arithmetic then runs whatever it comes to. So a log scale asked for `-5` answers `NaN` — a perfectly good number with no logarithm — where the same scale asked for a *word* answers nothing at all. Reading the answer instead of the input conflates the two, and the empty cell is what separates them: it coerces to `0`, passes the guard, and its logarithm is `NaN` too. The negative row is here for that one distinction.

text.signal: datum.what + ' -> ' + scale('y', datum.v) + ' | q ' + scale('q', datum.v) + ' | th ' + scale('th', datum.v) + ' | qt ' + scale('qt', datum.v) + ' | o ' + scale('o', datum.v) + ' | e ' + scale('e', 'a') + ' | lg ' + scale('lg', datum.v)
